title: Card surcharge ban signals cash is back
full_text:
Just when you’ve become comfortable carrying little or no cash in your purse, wallet or smartphone cover, dollars and cents are set to burst back into popularity for consumers and businesses.
The Reserve Bank’s ban on card surcharges is prompting expectations of a comeback for cash in the economy, with more businesses to offer cash discounts or enforce cash-only policies that shift customers away from paying with credit and debit cards.
The biggest shock to the system could be for today’s young adults, who have grown up in an effectively cashless economy dominated by tap-and-go, digital banking and e-commerce transactions.
Current credit card surcharges are typically between 1 per cent and 1.5 per cent, and the RBA says from October 1 these will no longer be permitted for Eftpos, Visa, Mastercard, American Express, PayPal and UnionPay. Business owners will have to wear the cost of their customers using cards unless they pass it on through higher prices.
Chartered account Raj Kuckreja, co-founder of accounts receivable business intelligence platform ezyCollect, said he was already seeing more retailers promoting discounts for customers to pay with cash.
“From a business owner’s perspective, there is a logic to that,” Mr Kuckreja said. “If card acceptance has a cost, increasing prices for every customer means people who pay with cash or other lower-cost methods are effectively contributing to the cost of card payments as well.” Mr Kuckreja said price was a powerful motivator and if cash discounts became common and meaningful, consumers could “respond quite quickly”.
He said there was now a generation of young consumers who found carrying cash “almost completely foreign”.
“They are used to tapping a phone or card and may not even think about things such as carrying the right amount of cash, receiving change or managing physical money,” he said. “I don’t think we are going back to a predominantly cash economy, but discounts can certainly change behaviour at the margins.” Both the RBA and Australian Competition & Consumer Commission have made it clear to business owners that giving discounts to people who pay with cash is acceptable.
The ACCC says “businesses can offer discounts to consumers who pay using a particular payment method, such as cash or PayID”.
“Payment method discounts should be clearly disclosed before consumers choose to book, order or pay,” it says.
The RBA has urged business owners to shop around for different payment service providers, work with them to understand payment costs, and promote other options.
“Businesses that wish to steer consumers towards other payment methods can do so by providing discounts instead of using surcharges,” it says.
An analysis by Cash Welcome has found that there are an average $3869 of cash notes on issue for every Australian today. This is less than a third of the value of notes held per person in Germany, Singapore and Switzerland, but more than people living in the US, Canada, Britain, China and New Zealand.
Cash Welcome campaign manager Jason Bryce said he expected to see more cash-only businesses.
“I think it’s an unintended consequence of the move on October 1 that there’s going to be more cash, there’s going to be more people carrying cash, and I’m predicting a new all-time record in the amount of cash in circulation,” Mr Bryce said.
“I think we’re seeing a comeback for cash.” Some young people would start carrying cash for the first time, Mr Bryce said. “It doesn’t take every single business to go cash-only – it only takes a few, and then you think ‘I might need cash so I better have a little’,” he said.
